question: Alec controls [Elspeth Conquers Death] and puts the third lore counter it. With the triggered ability, they target [Eternal Witness] in their graveyard. When Eternal Witness returns to the battlefield, can it target Elspeth Conquers Death with its trigger?
answer:
Direct answer: Yes — Eternal Witness can target Elspeth Conquers Death, because the Saga is already in Alec's graveyard by the time Eternal Witness's trigger is put on the stack and its target chosen.

Important honesty note: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts provided to me address Saga sacrifice timing or when a triggered ability's targets are chosen. The only grounding I have is the card rulings supplied with the card data, which do directly settle it:

- "Once the number of lore counters on a Saga is greater than or equal to the greatest number among its chapter abilities, the Saga's controller sacrifices it as soon as its chapter ability has left the stack, most likely by resolving or being countered. This state-based action doesn't use the stack." [Elspeth Conquers Death ruling #11] — so Elspeth Conquers Death goes to the graveyard immediately upon chapter III finishing resolution, before any player gets priority and before Eternal Witness's trigger is placed on the stack with its target.
- The analogous case: "If a resolving spell puts Eternal Witness onto the battlefield, Eternal Witness's ability can target that card if it's put into your graveyard as it resolves." [Eternal Witness ruling #0]

Secondary points: Eternal Witness returns the card to Alec's hand, so Alec must recast Elspeth Conquers Death for {3}{W}{W} to reuse it. Chapter III also puts a +1/+1 counter or loyalty counter on the returned Eternal Witness; a loyalty counter on a creature normally does nothing [Elspeth Conquers Death ruling #8]. Nothing about this interaction differs between a two-player game and a multiplayer table.

If you want this confirmed against the numbered rules on triggered-ability targeting (601.2c/603.3) and state-based actions (704), those rules were not included in my context, so I can't cite them.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.603.3: Once an ability has triggered, its controller puts it on the stack as an object that’s not a card the next time a player would receive priority. See rule 117, “Timing and Priority.” The ability becomes the topmost object on the stack. It has the text of the ability that created it, and no other characteristics. It remains on the stack until it’s countered, it resolves, a rule causes it to be removed from the stack, or an effect moves it elsewhere.
gold_text.704.5s: The state-based actions are as follows: If the number of lore counters on a Saga permanent with one or more chapter abilities is greater than or equal to its final chapter number and it isn’t the source of a chapter ability that has triggered but not yet left the stack, that Saga’s controller sacrifices it. See rule 714, “Saga Cards.”
gold_text.714.4: If the number of lore counters on a Saga permanent with one or more chapter abilities is greater than or equal to its final chapter number, and it isn’t the source of a chapter ability that has triggered but not yet left the stack, that Saga’s controller sacrifices it. This state-based action doesn’t use the stack.

answer_gold:
Yes.

When the final chapter ability resolves, Eternal Witness is returned to the battlefield. However, its triggered ability is not put onto the stack until after state based actions are checked. When state based actions are checked, Elspeth Conquers Death is sacrificed because is has a number of lore counters greater than or equal to its final chapter number. After this, triggers are placed onto the stack, and Elspeth Conquers Death is in the graveyard able to be the target of Eternal Witness's triggered ability.

question: Autumn attacks with [Robber of the Rich], exiling [Light Up the Stage] from Nehemiah's library. Can Autumn pay Light Up the Stage's Spectacle cost with only {C}?
answer:
Honest answer: the Comprehensive Rules text I was given doesn't settle this. Every rule provided here concerns copying objects, merging permanents, layers, and replacement-effect ordering (707.x, 730.2a, 613.2a, 616.1f, 110.5c, 607.5a, 712.21b) — none of it addresses mana, mana costs, or what "you may spend mana as though it were mana of any color" does to colorless {C} mana. None of the supplied Light Up the Stage or Robber of the Rich rulings addresses colorless mana either. So I can't verifiably resolve whether one {C} can pay Spectacle {R} from what's in front of me.

What the provided card text and rulings do establish:
- Light Up the Stage's Spectacle cost is {R} — a single red mana, with no generic component. Light Up the Stage ruling #5 confirms you begin from the alternative (spectacle) cost you're paying, then add increases and apply reductions; note that a reduction of generic mana could never touch a cost that is purely {R}.
- Robber of the Rich's text grants Autumn permission to cast the exiled card and to "spend mana as though it were mana of any color to cast that spell." What the provided material does not tell me is whether colorless mana counts as "mana" that can be spent as though it were mana of any color; the symbol note I was given says only that {C} is never satisfied by colored mana, which is not the same question.
- Regardless of the mana question, Autumn must have attacked with a Rogue (Robber of the Rich itself is a Rogue), and this works even if Robber of the Rich has left combat or the battlefield (Robber of the Rich rulings #3 and #5).
- Spectacle needs an opponent to have lost life this turn; damage counts as life loss (Light Up the Stage ruling #4), and it only matters that life was lost, not that the total is still lower (Light Up the Stage ruling #6). Combat damage from Robber of the Rich to Nehemiah would satisfy this.
- Timing is unchanged: Light Up the Stage is a sorcery, castable only in Autumn's main phase with an empty stack (Robber of the Rich ruling #6, Light Up the Stage ruling #8) — here, the postcombat main phase.
- Multiplayer: the defending player whose library is exiled from is the player attacked, or the controller of an attacked planeswalker (Robber of the Rich ruling #9); with more than two players, Spectacle needs only some opponent to have lost life, even one who later left the game (Light Up the Stage ruling #3).

To settle the {C} question I'd need the rules on paying mana costs and on "spend mana as though it were mana of any color" (roughly the 601.2g / 609.4-type rules), which weren't provided.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.118.9a: Some spells have alternative costs. An alternative cost is a cost listed in a spell’s text, or applied to it from another effect, that its controller may pay rather than paying the spell’s mana cost. Alternative costs are usually phrased, “You may [action] rather than pay [this object’s] mana cost,” or “You may cast [this object] without paying its mana cost.” Note that some alternative costs are listed in keywords; see rule 702. Only one alternative cost can be applied to any one spell as it’s being cast. The controller of the spell announces their intentions to pay that cost as described in rule 601.2b.
gold_text.609.4b: Some effects state that a player may do something “as though” some condition were true or a creature can do something “as though” some condition were true. This applies only to the stated effect. For purposes of that effect, treat the game exactly as if the stated condition were true. For all other purposes, treat the game normally. If an effect allows a player to spend mana “as though it were mana of any [type or color],” this affects only how the player may pay a cost. It doesn’t change that cost, and it doesn’t change what mana was actually spent to pay that cost. The same is true for effects that say “mana of any type can be spent.”
gold_text.702.137a: Spectacle Spectacle is a static ability that functions on the stack. “Spectacle [cost]” means “You may pay [cost] rather than pay this spell’s mana cost if an opponent lost life this turn.” Casting a spell for its spectacle cost follows the rules for paying alternative costs in rules 601.2b and 601.2f–h.

answer_gold:
Yes.

Robber of the Rich allows Autumn to cast the card and "may spend mana as though it were mana of any color to cast that spell." This changes how the player may pay a cost, and they can do so with any mana, regardless of color. 

"Spectacle" is an alternative cost ([702.137a]), and can only be used if no other alternative cost is being paid. Luckily, Robber of the Rich does not create an alternative cost, it just changes how mana may be spent.

question: Nico controls [Urza's Saga] with two lore counters on it. Alexzander uses [Jinx] to change its land type. What happens?
answer:
Short answer: the provided context doesn't contain the rule needed to settle this (the rule on how changing a land's subtype affects its other types and intrinsic abilities, i.e. rule 305.7), so I can't tell you definitively whether Urza's Saga keeps its Saga type and chapter abilities after Jinx resolves.

What the provided material does establish:
- Jinx reads "Target land becomes the basic land type of your choice until end of turn," so Alexzander chooses one basic land type for Nico's Urza's Saga, and it is a type-changing/subtype-setting effect that lasts until end of turn.
- Abilities Urza's Saga already gained from its chapter I and chapter II abilities stay with it for as long as it's on the battlefield [Urza's Saga ruling #5]. So a previously gained "{T}: Add {C}" (from chapter I) — note {C} is colorless mana specifically, not generic — and the Construct-token ability (from chapter II, cost "{2}, {T}", where {2} is two generic mana) would not be stripped by Jinx.
- If Urza's Saga were to lose all of its chapter abilities while still being a Saga, it would immediately be sacrificed [Urza's Saga ruling #1]. Conversely, as long as it is still a Saga it will be sacrificed after its last chapter ability resolves, land or not [Urza's Saga ruling #4].

What's missing: the rule text governing whether setting a basic land type overwrites the "Urza's Saga" land subtype and/or the Saga enchantment subtype, and whether the printed chapter abilities are removed. Without that rule in context I won't guess, because the outcome (nothing much happens vs. immediate sacrifice) hinges entirely on it.

Timing note: I'm assuming Jinx resolves while Urza's Saga has exactly two lore counters and before Nico's next draw step adds the third. If instead Jinx resolves after the third lore counter and chapter III has already resolved, Urza's Saga is sacrificed as a state-based action regardless [Urza's Saga ruling #4].

The two-player vs. multiplayer distinction doesn't matter here; nothing in the provided rules makes this interaction depend on the number of players.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.205.1a: The type line is printed directly below the illustration. It contains the card’s card type(s). It also contains the card’s subtype(s) and supertype(s), if applicable. Some effects set an object’s card type. In most such cases, the new card type(s) replaces any existing card types. However, an object with either the instant or sorcery card type retains that type. Counters, stickers, effects, and damage marked on the object remain with it, even if they are meaningless to the new card type. Similarly, when an effect sets one or more of an object’s subtypes, the new subtype(s) replaces any existing subtypes from the appropriate set (creature types, land types, artifact types, enchantment types, planeswalker types, or spell types). If an object’s card type is removed, the subtypes correlated with that card type will remain if they are also the subtypes of a card type the object currently has; otherwise, they are also removed for the entire time the object’s card type is removed. Removing an object’s subtype doesn’t affect its card types at all.
gold_text.305.7: If an effect sets a land’s subtype to one or more of the basic land types, the land no longer has its old land type. It loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and any copiable effects affecting that land, and it gains the appropriate mana ability for each new basic land type. Note that this doesn’t remove any abilities that were granted to the land by other effects. Setting a land’s subtype doesn’t add or remove any card types (such as creature) or supertypes (such as basic, legendary, and snow) the land may have. If a land gains one or more land types in addition to its own, it keeps its land types and rules text, and it gains the new land types and mana abilities.
gold_text.505.4: Second, if the active player controls one or more Saga enchantments and it’s the active player’s precombat main phase, the active player puts a lore counter on each Saga they control with one or more chapter abilities. (See rule 714, “Saga Cards.”) This turn-based action doesn’t use the stack.
gold_text.611.2c: A continuous effect may be generated by the resolution of a spell or ability. If a continuous effect generated by the resolution of a spell or ability modifies the characteristics or changes the controller of any objects, the set of objects it affects is determined when that continuous effect begins. After that point, the set won’t change. (Note that this works differently than a continuous effect from a static ability.) A continuous effect generated by the resolution of a spell or ability that doesn’t modify the characteristics or change the controller of any objects modifies the rules of the game, so it can affect objects that weren’t affected when that continuous effect began. If a single continuous effect has parts that modify the characteristics or changes the controller of any objects and other parts that don’t, the set of objects each part applies to is determined independently. An effect that reads “All white creatures get +1/+1 until end of turn” gives the bonus to all permanents that are white creatures when the spell or ability resolves—even if they change color later—and doesn’t affect those that enter the battlefield or turn white afterward. An effect that reads “Prevent all damage creatures would deal this turn” doesn’t modify any object’s characteristics, so it’s modifying the rules of the game. That means the effect will apply even to damage from creatures that weren’t on the battlefield when the continuous effect began. It also affects damage from permanents that become creatures later in the turn.
gold_text.613.1d: The values of an object’s characteristics are determined by starting with the actual object. For a card, that means the values of the characteristics printed on that card. For a token or a copy of a spell or card, that means the values of the characteristics defined by the effect that created it. Then all applicable continuous effects are applied in a series of layers in the following order: Layer 4: Type-changing effects are applied. These include effects that change an object’s card type, subtype, and/or supertype.
gold_text.613.1f: The values of an object’s characteristics are determined by starting with the actual object. For a card, that means the values of the characteristics printed on that card. For a token or a copy of a spell or card, that means the values of the characteristics defined by the effect that created it. Then all applicable continuous effects are applied in a series of layers in the following order: Layer 6: Ability-adding effects, keyword counters, ability-removing effects, and effects that say an object can’t have an ability are applied.
gold_text.703.4f: The turn-based actions are as follows: Immediately after a player’s precombat main phase begins, that player puts a lore counter on each Saga enchantment they control with one or more chapter abilities. In an Archenemy game, this happens after the archenemy’s scheme action. See rule 714, “Saga Cards.”
gold_text.704.5s: The state-based actions are as follows: If the number of lore counters on a Saga permanent with one or more chapter abilities is greater than or equal to its final chapter number and it isn’t the source of a chapter ability that has triggered but not yet left the stack, that Saga’s controller sacrifices it. See rule 714, “Saga Cards.”
gold_text.714.3b: Sagas use lore counters to track their progress. Each Saga with read ahead has the intrinsic abilities “As this Saga enters, choose a number between one and this Saga’s final chapter number” and “This Saga enters with the chosen number of lore counters on it.” (See rule 702.155, “Read Ahead.”) These abilities create replacement effects (see rule 614.1c).
gold_text.714.4: If the number of lore counters on a Saga permanent with one or more chapter abilities is greater than or equal to its final chapter number, and it isn’t the source of a chapter ability that has triggered but not yet left the stack, that Saga’s controller sacrifices it. This state-based action doesn’t use the stack.

answer_gold:
In layer 4, Urza's Saga will have its land type overwritten as well as lose all of its chapter abilities. It will gain the abilities to tap for {C} and to create Construct tokens in layer 6, as those abilities are granted by a continuous effect that was generated when the previous chapter abilities resolved..

Because Urza's Saga has lost all of its chapter abilities while still being a Saga, it is immediately sacrificed the next time state-based actions are checked, per the Urza's Saga ruling "If Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, perhaps due to a card like Blood Moon, it will immediately be sacrificed".

question: Ada controls [Ethersworn Canonist]. They want to suspend [Shade of Trokair] and then cast [Divination]. Can they?
answer:
Yes — Ada can suspend Shade of Trokair and then cast Divination, assuming they haven't already cast a nonartifact spell this turn and are acting at a time they could cast Shade of Trokair (their own main phase, empty stack).

I want to be explicit about my grounding: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts provided to me address this interaction at all — they cover myriad (702.116a-b), ending the turn or combat phase (724.1a-f, 724.2a-e), the end of combat step (511.1-511.2), the cleanup step (514.2, 703.4p), and step/phase-based effect expiry (500.4, 500.5). So I am not citing any numbered rule, because none of the ones I was given are relevant.

What does settle it is the provided card data and rulings, which the instructions treat as authoritative on their own:
- Exiling a card with suspend isn't casting that card; it doesn't use the stack and can't be responded to [Shade of Trokair ruling #7]. So suspending Shade of Trokair does not count as casting a nonartifact spell.
- Ethersworn Canonist's own text stops a player who has cast a nonartifact spell this turn from casting additional nonartifact spells; each player may cast any number of artifact spells plus a maximum of one nonartifact spell per turn [Ethersworn Canonist ruling #1]. Since suspending isn't casting, Divination is still Ada's first nonartifact spell and is legal.

Caveat on ordering: you may only exile a card with suspend at a time you could actually cast it, considering effects that stop you from casting it [Shade of Trokair ruling #2]. If Ada had already cast a nonartifact spell earlier in the turn, Ethersworn Canonist would prevent casting Shade of Trokair and thus also prevent suspending it. In the reverse order (Divination first), Ada could not then suspend Shade of Trokair.

Ethersworn Canonist is symmetrical, so in a multiplayer game each other player is likewise limited to one nonartifact spell per turn; Ada's situation is unchanged by player count.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.702.62a: Suspend Suspend is a keyword that represents three abilities. The first is a static ability that functions while the card with suspend is in a player’s hand. The second and third are triggered abilities that function in the exile zone. “Suspend N—[cost]” means “If you could begin to cast this card by putting it onto the stack from your hand, you may pay [cost] and exile it with N time counters on it. This action doesn’t use the stack,” and “At the beginning of your upkeep, if this card is suspended, remove a time counter from it,” and “When the last time counter is removed from this card, if it’s exiled, you may play it without paying its mana cost if able. If you don’t, it remains exiled. If you cast a creature spell this way, it gains haste until you lose control of the spell or the permanent it becomes.”

answer_gold: Yes. Suspending a card is not casting a spell, so it does not count towards Ethersworn Canonist's restriction.

question: Asa controls an [Inventors' Fair], a [Krark-Clan Ironworks], and two [Piston Sledge]. They want to activate the last ability of Inventors' Fair and sacrifice a Piston Sledge to help pay the cost. Is this legal?
answer:
Direct answer: Yes, it's legal — but I should be transparent about my grounding. The numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts provided to me in this conversation are all about Saga cards and lore counters (714.x, 703.4f, 505.4, 704.5s), layers (613.6), land subtypes (305.7), supertypes (205.4b), and text-changing effects (612.2). None of those rules address activated-ability costs, activation restrictions, or when costs are paid, so the numbered rules text I was given does not settle this question.

What does settle it is the card data I was given, which counts as ground truth: Inventors' Fair's last ability reads "{4}, {T}, Sacrifice Inventors' Fair: Search your library for an artifact card, reveal it, put it into your hand, then shuffle. Activate only if you control three or more artifacts," and its ruling states that the number of artifacts you control is checked only as you activate the ability, not again as it resolves [Inventors' Fair ruling #2]. Asa controls three artifacts at activation — Krark-Clan Ironworks and the two Piston Sledge (Inventors' Fair is a Legendary Land, not an artifact) — so the restriction is met. Asa may then use Krark-Clan Ironworks ("Sacrifice an artifact: Add {C}{C}"), sacrificing one Piston Sledge, and apply that {C}{C} to the {4} generic portion of the cost; generic mana accepts colorless mana. Two more mana of any type are still needed for the {4}, along with {T} and sacrificing Inventors' Fair itself.

Because the artifact count isn't rechecked, dropping to two artifacts while paying costs doesn't invalidate the activation. Nothing here involves opponents or turn order, so this works identically at a two-player and a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.601.2: To cast a spell is to take it from where it is (usually the hand), put it on the stack, and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. Casting a spell includes proposal of the spell (rules 601.2a–d) and determination and payment of costs (rules 601.2f–h). To cast a spell, a player follows the steps listed below, in order. A player must be legally allowed to cast the spell to begin this process (see rule 601.3). If a player is unable to comply with the requirements of a step listed below while performing that step, the casting of the spell is illegal; the game returns to the moment before the casting of that spell was proposed (see rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions”).
gold_text.601.2g: To cast a spell is to take it from where it is (usually the hand), put it on the stack, and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. Casting a spell includes proposal of the spell (rules 601.2a–d) and determination and payment of costs (rules 601.2f–h). To cast a spell, a player follows the steps listed below, in order. A player must be legally allowed to cast the spell to begin this process (see rule 601.3). If a player is unable to comply with the requirements of a step listed below while performing that step, the casting of the spell is illegal; the game returns to the moment before the casting of that spell was proposed (see rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions”). If the total cost includes a mana payment, the player then has a chance to activate mana abilities (see rule 605, “Mana Abilities”). Mana abilities must be activated before costs are paid.
gold_text.602.2b: To activate an ability is to put it onto the stack and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. Only an object’s controller (or its owner, if it doesn’t have a controller) can activate its activated ability unless the object specifically says otherwise. Activating an ability follows the steps listed below, in order. If, at any point during the activation of an ability, a player is unable to comply with any of those steps, the activation is illegal; the game returns to the moment before that ability started to be activated (see rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions”). Announcements and payments can’t be altered after they’ve been made. The remainder of the process for activating an ability is identical to the process for casting a spell listed in rules 601.2b–i. Those rules apply to activating an ability just as they apply to casting a spell. An activated ability’s analog to a spell’s mana cost (as referenced in rule 601.2f) is its activation cost.

answer_gold: Yes. The process for activating an ability is the same as the process for casting a spell. It must be legal to activate the ability in order to put it onto the stack. Mana abilities are only activated after the legality of activating the original ability has been checked.

question: Amare controls [Psychogenic Probe] and casts [Pain], targeting Nico. They discard a [Progenitus]. Does Psychogenic Probe trigger?
answer:
Direct answer, unchanged: Yes — Psychogenic Probe triggers and deals 2 damage to Nico.

On grounding: the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given are all about combat (declaring attackers, creatures put onto the battlefield attacking, removal from combat, reselecting what a creature attacks). None of them address discarding, replacement effects, shuffling a library, or triggered abilities of this kind, so I am not resting this answer on any of them and I won't cite one I didn't use.

What does settle it is the card text and rulings provided:
- Pain (the {B} half of the split card) says "Target player discards a card," so Nico discards Progenitus, and a split card counts as one card discarded [Pain // Suffering ruling #0].
- Progenitus says "If Progenitus would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, reveal Progenitus and shuffle it into its owner's library instead." That card text replaces the graveyard placement with Nico shuffling their library.
- Psychogenic Probe says "Whenever a spell or ability causes a player to shuffle their library, this artifact deals 2 damage to that player." Progenitus's ability is what caused the shuffle, so Psychogenic Probe triggers and the 2 damage goes to the player who shuffled — Nico — not to Amare, even though Amare controls Psychogenic Probe and cast Pain. It would trigger even if Nico's library were empty [Psychogenic Probe ruling #0].

Progenitus's protection from everything doesn't stop this: Pain targets the player, and the 2 damage is dealt to Nico rather than to Progenitus [Progenitus ruling #0], [Progenitus ruling #1]. This is assuming Progenitus is Nico's own card, so "its owner's library" is Nico's library. The result is the same whether the game has two players or more.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.614.6: If an event is replaced, it never happens. A modified event occurs instead, which may in turn trigger abilities. Note that the modified event may contain instructions that can’t be carried out, in which case the impossible instruction is simply ignored.

answer_gold: Yes. Progenitus's replacement effect changes the effect of Pain from "Nico discards a card, putting it into their graveyard" to "Nico reveals a card and shuffles it into their library". Pain still caused the shuffle, so Psychogenic Probe triggers.

question: Albert controls [Doubling Season] and [Pir, Imaginative Rascal] and activates the +1 ability of [Ajani, Mentor of Heroes]. How many loyalty counters does it gain?
answer:
Honest correction: the numbered Comprehensive Rules text provided to me in this conversation does not cover this question at all. Every numbered rule given above concerns damage, life gain, lifelink, and Two-Headed Giant life totals (119.3, 119.9, 119.10, 120.3a, 120.3f, 120.4d, 702.15a–f, 810.9g). None of them address counters, replacement effects that multiply counters, or the distinction between paying a cost and applying an effect. So I cannot ground this answer in the numbered rules I was given, and I'm setting answered to false rather than inventing a citation.

What I can point to is the card data provided: Doubling Season's ruling states that if you activate an ability whose cost has you put loyalty counters on a planeswalker, that number isn't doubled, because those counters are put on as a cost rather than as an effect. Pir, Imaginative Rascal's text is likewise a replacement for counters an effect would put on a permanent. On that basis Ajani, Mentor of Heroes would receive just one loyalty counter for the "+1" activation cost. Treat that as resting on the card rulings, not on the rules text supplied here.

What's missing from the context to fully settle it: the rules on activation costs and loyalty abilities, and the rule on applying replacement effects to counters being placed.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.606.4: The cost to activate a loyalty ability of a permanent is to put on or remove from that permanent a certain number of loyalty counters, as shown by the loyalty symbol in the ability’s cost. This cost may be modified by other effects.
gold_text.609.1: An effect is something that happens in the game as a result of a spell or ability. When a spell, activated ability, or triggered ability resolves, it may create one or more one-shot or continuous effects. Static abilities may create one or more continuous effects. Text itself is never an effect.
gold_text.614.16: Some replacement effects apply “if an effect would create one or more tokens” or “if an effect would put one or more counters on a permanent.” These replacement effects apply if the effect of a resolving spell or ability creates a token or puts a counter on a permanent, and they also apply if another replacement or prevention effect does so, even if the original event being modified wasn’t itself an effect.

answer_gold:
Four.

Activating a planeswalker ability includes paying the loyalty cost, which in this case means adding one loyalty counter. Doubling Season only replaces effects, which are the result of a spell or ability. However Pir, Imaginative Rascal replaces the original one loyalty counter with two, which Doubling Season can then replace with doubling the additional loyalty counters, resulting in a total of four.

question: Aminah casts a [Show and Tell]. As it resolves, Aminah chooses to put a [Haru-Onna] onto the battlefield and Nico chooses to put a [Domestication] onto the battlefield enchanting Haru-Onna. Who controls the enters-the-battlefield ability of Haru-Onna?
answer:
Honest answer: the numbered Comprehensive Rules text provided to me does not settle this. The rules excerpts I was given cover card draws from empty libraries, state-based actions, searching outside the game, the Ring tempting you, collecting evidence, rolling the planar die, and mana of undefined types. None of them address who controls a permanent that enters the battlefield, who controls a triggered ability, how Auras that say "You control enchanted creature" grant control, or how simultaneous entries are handled. To answer definitively I would need the rules on controller of a triggered ability (the ability's controller being the controller of its source) and on control-changing continuous effects from Auras — those were not provided.

What the provided card data does establish, without me guessing at rules:
- Show and Tell's rulings say players choose during resolution, the active player (Aminah) chooses first and each other player chooses in turn order, choices required by the entering cards (such as what Domestication enchants) are made after all card choices, and the cards are then put onto the battlefield simultaneously [Show and Tell ruling #0], [Show and Tell ruling #1], [Show and Tell ruling #2].
- Domestication's own text reads "You control enchanted creature," and its rulings confirm it can enchant a creature regardless of power, with power checked only when its end-step ability triggers and resolves [Domestication ruling #0], [Domestication ruling #1].
- Haru-Onna's text is "When this creature enters, draw a card."

So Domestication is on the battlefield enchanting Haru-Onna from the same instant Haru-Onna arrives, meaning Nico has control of Haru-Onna at that moment — which points strongly toward Nico controlling the draw trigger. But I can't cite a provided rule for the "controller of the permanent controls its enters trigger" step, so I'm flagging this as not fully grounded rather than presenting it as settled.

This discussion assumes Show and Tell resolved as described; if Domestication had instead been cast after Haru-Onna was already on the battlefield, Haru-Onna's enters trigger would have already been put on the stack under Aminah's control. Show and Tell affects each player, so with more than two players each additional player also chooses in turn order after Aminah.

gold_text.303.4f: Some enchantments have the subtype “Aura.” An Aura enters the battlefield attached to an object or player. What an Aura can be attached to is defined by its enchant keyword ability (see rule 702.5, “Enchant”). Other effects can limit what a permanent can be enchanted by. If an Aura is entering the battlefield under a player’s control by any means other than by resolving as an Aura spell, and the effect putting it onto the battlefield doesn’t specify the object or player the Aura will enchant, that player chooses what it will enchant as the Aura enters the battlefield. The player must choose a legal object or player according to the Aura’s enchant ability and any other applicable effects.

answer_gold: This can't happen as described. Nico must choose a permanent that is already on the battlefield for the Domestication to enchant. They can't choose a permanent that is entering at the same time.

question:
Amani controls a [Founding the Third Path], and its third ability is resolving. Amani chooses to cast a [Fatal Push] from their graveyard. Amani currently does not have Revolt.
Can Amani choose to target [Skyhunter Patrol] with Fatal Push? Will Skyhunter Patrol be destroyed by Fatal Push?
answer:
Correction on sourcing: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given (they cover counters, piles, manifest, amass, connive, shuffling, merged permanents, timestamps) bear on this question at all, so I cannot cite any rule number here. My answer rests entirely on the card text and the provided card rulings, which the instructions treat as authoritative grounding on their own.

Direct answer: Yes, Amani can target Skyhunter Patrol with Fatal Push, and no, Skyhunter Patrol will not be destroyed.

- Legality of the target: Fatal Push may target any creature, even one with a high mana value; the mana value is checked only when Fatal Push resolves [Fatal Push ruling #3]. Skyhunter Patrol, a 2/3 Cat Knight with mana cost {2}{W}{W} and mana value 4, is therefore a legal target.
- Result on resolution: Fatal Push's printed text destroys the target only if it has mana value 2 or less; the Revolt clause would raise that to mana value 4 or less, but only if a permanent left the battlefield under Amani's control this turn. Amani does not have Revolt, so Skyhunter Patrol's mana value 4 is too high and it is not destroyed.
- Casting via Founding the Third Path: chapter III exiles the Fatal Push card from Amani's graveyard, copies it, and Amani may cast the copy — but Amani must do so as the chapter ability resolves and must pay the copy's costs, i.e. {B}, since chapter III does not say "without paying its mana cost" [Founding the Third Path ruling #2].
- Why Revolt still isn't on: Revolt cares only that a permanent left the battlefield under your control, regardless of cause or destination [Fatal Push ruling #2], and tokens count too [Fatal Push ruling #0]. Exiling Fatal Push from the graveyard is not a permanent leaving the battlefield, and Founding the Third Path's read-ahead "Sacrifice after III" happens only after that chapter ability has finished resolving — after the copy has already been cast and resolved. If instead some permanent had already left the battlefield under Amani's control earlier in the turn, Revolt would be satisfied and Skyhunter Patrol would be destroyed.

This outcome does not depend on the number of players; it is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.714.4: If the number of lore counters on a Saga permanent with one or more chapter abilities is greater than or equal to its final chapter number, and it isn’t the source of a chapter ability that has triggered but not yet left the stack, that Saga’s controller sacrifices it. This state-based action doesn’t use the stack.

answer_gold:
Yes Amani can target Skyhunter Patrol, and it will be destroyed by Fatal Push.

Fatal Push does not check for the target's mana value when put on the stack, so Amani is allowed to target Skyhunter Patrol.

Amani will put Fatal Push on the stack as part of the resolution of Founding the Third Path's third chapter. Once the ability is done resolving, SBAs are checked and the saga is sacrificed. In particular this means that Amani will have Revolt when Fatal Push resolves, thus Skyhunter Patrol will get destroyed.

question: Ari controls [Bludgeon Brawl] and [Soldevi Digger]. They cast [Titania's Song]. Once it resolves, what are the characteristics of Soldevi Digger?
answer:
Direct answer, unchanged: Soldevi Digger becomes a 2/2 artifact creature with no abilities, and it is no longer an Equipment.

On sourcing: none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts provided in this conversation are relevant here — they cover +1/+1 counter mechanics (devour, scavenge, amass, adapt, bloodthirst, escape, backup, increment, ravenous), replacement effects that modify how permanents enter the battlefield [614.13b], and state-based actions with last known information [704.8]. So I am not citing any rule number, because none of the ones I was given settles this. My answer rests entirely on the provided card text and rulings, which do directly cover it:

- Titania's Song's own text: "Each noncreature artifact loses all abilities and becomes an artifact creature with power and toughness each equal to its mana value." Soldevi Digger's mana value is 2 ({2}), so it becomes a 2/2 artifact creature and loses "{2}: Put the top card of your graveyard on the bottom of your library."
- Bludgeon Brawl's own text applies only to "each noncreature, non-Equipment artifact," so once Soldevi Digger is a creature, Bludgeon Brawl no longer grants it equip {2} or "Equipped creature gets +2/+0." [Bludgeon Brawl ruling #2] states this explicitly: an affected artifact that later becomes a creature stops being an Equipment and becomes unattached from any creature it was attached to, while remaining on the battlefield. [Bludgeon Brawl ruling #3] adds that an Equipment that's also a creature can't be equipped to anything.
- Titania's Song's text also says that if it leaves the battlefield, the effect continues until end of turn, so destroying Titania's Song this turn won't restore Soldevi Digger's ability or Equipment status until the turn ends.
- [Titania's Song ruling #0]: Soldevi Digger can attack only if Ari has continuously controlled it since the beginning of their most recent turn; how long it has been a creature doesn't matter.

This is player-count independent, so it's the same in a two-player game or multiplayer.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.613.8a: Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is sometimes done using a dependency system. If a dependency exists, it will override the timestamp system. An effect is said to “depend on” another if (a) it’s applied in the same layer (and, if applicable, sublayer) as the other effect; (b) applying the other would change the text or the existence of the first effect, what it applies to, or what it does to any of the things it applies to; and (c) neither effect is from a characteristic-defining ability or both effects are from characteristic-defining abilities. Otherwise, the effect is considered to be independent of the other effect.

answer_gold: It's a 2/2 artifact creature with no abilities. Applying Titania's Song would cause Bludgeon Brawl to no longer apply (since Soldevi Digger would be a creature). However, applying Bludgeon Brawl would not change how Titania's Song's effect is applied, so Bludgeon Brawl is dependent on Titania's Song. Titania's Song applies first, and then Bludgeon Brawl won't affect Soldevi Digger since it's a creature.

question: Audrey casts [Enlarge] targeting [Goblin Piker], and then attacks with the Goblin Piker. Nico blocks it with a [Baron Sengir], which has gained infect due to their [Grafted Exoskeleton] and indestructible due to their [Withstand Death]. What happens at the end of the turn?
answer:
Short answer: Goblin Piker dies at the end of the turn, and Baron Sengir survives and gets a +2/+2 counter.

Why:

1. In combat, Goblin Piker is 9/8 (2/1 plus Enlarge's +7/+7) with trample, and Baron Sengir is 7/7 (5/5 plus Grafted Exoskeleton's +2/+2) with infect and indestructible from Withstand Death.
2. Baron Sengir's 7 damage to Goblin Piker isn't marked as damage — because of infect it's dealt as seven -1/-1 counters instead [Grafted Exoskeleton ruling #3] (infect applies to any damage). Goblin Piker is therefore 2/1 during combat (9/8 minus seven) and survives the combat damage step. Those -1/-1 counters stay on it permanently; they are not removed at end of turn and would not be removed by regeneration [Grafted Exoskeleton ruling #6].
3. Goblin Piker's own 9 damage to Baron Sengir does nothing lasting: Withstand Death makes Baron Sengir indestructible, so lethal damage doesn't destroy it, and its toughness is not reduced by damage.
4. When the turn ends, Enlarge's +7/+7 ends. Goblin Piker goes back to base 2/1 but still has seven -1/-1 counters, making it -5/-6. With toughness 0 or less it is put into the graveyard.
5. Goblin Piker was "dealt damage by Baron Sengir this turn" — infect damage is still damage in all respects, and abilities that trigger on damage being dealt do trigger [Grafted Exoskeleton ruling #2]. So Baron Sengir's ability ("Whenever a creature dealt damage by Baron Sengir this turn dies, put a +2/+2 counter on Baron Sengir") triggers and Baron Sengir ends up 8/8 (base 5/5, +2/+2 from Grafted Exoskeleton, +2/+2 counter), losing indestructible only when Withstand Death's until-end-of-turn effect ends.

Two gaps and one assumption I'll flag honestly:
- The rules excerpts provided here don't include the rules on the cleanup step, state-based actions for creatures with toughness 0 or less, or combat damage assignment/trample, so the precise timing (the +7/+7 wearing off in the cleanup step, Goblin Piker being put into the graveyard, and the resulting trigger being put on the stack with an extra round of priority) is stated from the card texts rather than from a numbered rule in this context. Grafted Exoskeleton ruling #5 does confirm such checks are state-based actions.
- I'm assuming no prevention effects were involved. If any of Baron Sengir's infect damage had been prevented, Goblin Piker would get correspondingly fewer -1/-1 counters and might survive the turn entirely [Grafted Exoskeleton ruling #7, 615.6].
- Enlarge also required Goblin Piker to be blocked if able, which is why Nico's block happened; if Baron Sengir hadn't been able to block, Goblin Piker would simply have been unblocked [Enlarge ruling #0].

Also: because Goblin Piker has trample and Baron Sengir is only 7 toughness, excess damage could be assigned to the defending player. Nothing in the provided rules covers trample assignment, so I can't quantify it from this context. In a two-player game that player is Nico; at a multiplayer table the defending player is whoever Audrey attacked, and only that player would take the trample damage — the rest of the table is unaffected.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.514.2: Second, the following actions happen simultaneously: all damage marked on permanents (including phased-out permanents) is removed and all “until end of turn” and “this turn” effects end. This turn-based action doesn’t use the stack.
gold_text.514.3a: Normally, no player receives priority during the cleanup step, so no spells can be cast and no abilities can be activated. However, this rule is subject to the following exception: At this point, the game checks to see if any state-based actions would be performed and/or any triggered abilities are waiting to be put onto the stack (including those that trigger “at the beginning of the next cleanup step”). If so, those state-based actions are performed, then those triggered abilities are put on the stack, then the active player gets priority. Players may cast spells and activate abilities. Once the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, another cleanup step begins.
gold_text.704.5f: The state-based actions are as follows: If a creature has toughness 0 or less, it’s put into its owner’s graveyard. Regeneration can’t replace this event.

cited_text.615.6: If damage that would be dealt is prevented, it never happens. A modified event may occur instead, which may in turn trigger abilities. Note that the modified event may contain instructions that can’t be carried out, in which case the impossible instruction is simply ignored.

answer_gold: The effect from Enlarge wears off, but the -1/-1 counters on Goblin Piker remain. Goblin Piker dies. It was dealt damage that turn by Baron Sengir, so Baron Sengir triggers.

question: Niko has a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] in their graveyard with 2 +1/+1 counters on it. Ashley controls [Containment Priest], and casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Niko. What happens?
answer:
Direct answer (unchanged): Skullbriar, the Walking Grave never enters the battlefield — Containment Priest exiles it instead, and Ashley gets no creatures from Ghastly Conscription.

Important transparency note on grounding: the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given in this conversation cover unrelated topics (losing/winning the game, ending the turn or combat phase, creatures put onto the battlefield attacking, multiplayer range of influence). None of them address manifesting, face-down permanents, replacement effects that exile an entering creature, or counters remaining on a card as it changes zones. So I am not citing any numbered rule here — my answer rests entirely on the card text and card rulings supplied as ground truth.

What that card material establishes:

1. Ghastly Conscription exiles all creature cards from Niko's graveyard in a face-down pile, shuffles it, then manifests them under Ashley's control (the caster). Manifesting puts a card onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2 creature with no name, mana cost, creature types, or abilities [Ghastly Conscription ruling #8], which its controller may turn face up for its mana cost if it's a creature card [Ghastly Conscription ruling #2].

2. Containment Priest reads "If a nontoken creature would enter and it wasn't cast, exile it instead." Skullbriar, the Walking Grave is a nontoken card that would be entering as a creature (the face-down manifested permanent is a 2/2 creature, per [Ghastly Conscription ruling #8]) and it was not cast — Ghastly Conscription put it onto the battlefield. Containment Priest ruling #1 confirms the exception only spares creatures that were actually cast, and Containment Priest ruling #3 confirms that what matters is whether the object is entering as a creature. So Skullbriar, the Walking Grave is exiled instead of entering the battlefield. The same happens to every other creature card Ghastly Conscription tries to manifest.

3. Since nothing enters the battlefield, nothing can be turned face up and no enters-the-battlefield abilities trigger. Containment Priest itself is unaffected (it was already on the battlefield; [Containment Priest ruling #0] and [Containment Priest ruling #2] are about it entering, which isn't happening here).

4. Counters: Skullbriar's own text, "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library," is card text that overrides the general rule about counters ceasing to exist on a zone change. It applies because Skullbriar had that ability in the zone it was leaving — Niko's graveyard [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1] — and it applies to all counters, not just +1/+1 counters [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #5]. So the two +1/+1 counters accompany it into exile, where it is a 2/2 [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2]. Those counters weren't "placed," so doubling effects wouldn't apply [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #0].

Honest limit: the provided material doesn't state whether the card retains its abilities while sitting face down in exile, so I can't say from what I was given whether those counters would survive a later move out of exile. It is revealed when it stops being face down [Ghastly Conscription ruling #11].

Player count doesn't change any of this; Ghastly Conscription simply targets the single player Niko regardless of table size.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.122.2: Counters on an object are not retained if that object moves from one zone to another. The counters are not “removed”; they simply cease to exist. See rule 400.7.
gold_text.406.7: If an object in the exile zone becomes exiled, it doesn’t change zones, but it becomes a new object that has just been exiled.
gold_text.701.40a: Manifest To manifest a card, turn it face down. It becomes a 2/2 face-down creature card with no text, no name, no subtypes, and no mana cost. Put that card onto the battlefield face down. That permanent is a manifested permanent for as long as it remains face down. The effect defining its characteristics works while the card is face down and ends when it’s turned face up.

answer_gold: In order for counters to remain on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, it needs to have that ability immediately before it changes zones. It did have that ability in the graveyard, so it is exiled face down with the +1/+1 counters remaining on it during that change. It then attempts to enter the battlefield, but remains in exile instead due to Containment Priest. Since it becomes a new object, it will be face-up in exile. However it didn't change zones, so the counters will remain on it in exile.

question: Ashley controls [Skill Borrower] and [Sensei's Divining Top]. The top card of their library is a [Putrid Leech]. Ashley activates Skill Borrower's ability, then activates Sensei's Divining Top's first ability, choosing to put Putrid Leech second from the top. Then they activate Sensei's Divining Top again, putting Putrid Leech back on top. Can Ashley activate Skill Borrower's ability again?
answer:
Honest answer: the Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given do not settle this question, so I can't rule on it with citations. The rules text provided here covers only power/toughness layers and sublayers (613.1g, 613.4a–d, 302.4c, 208.2a–b, 107.1b), tripling (701.11b), ingest (702.115a), meld pairs (712.5d), and glossary entries for Outlast and Base Power/Base Toughness. None of that addresses granted activated abilities, ability-activation timing/legality, or how an "Activate only once each turn" restriction is tracked — which is exactly what this question hinges on.

What I can say from the card text and rulings I was given, without a supporting numbered rule:
- Skill Borrower has "all activated abilities" of the top card of Ashley's library while that card is an artifact or creature card, so while Putrid Leech is on top, Skill Borrower has "Pay 2 life: This creature gets +2/+2 until end of turn. Activate only once each turn."
- While Putrid Leech is second from the top (and, say, a nonartifact noncreature card or Sensei's Divining Top is on top), Skill Borrower doesn't have that ability at all.
- The rulings note that if the top card changes while Ashley is activating a gained ability, the activation still works out even though Skill Borrower loses the ability [Skill Borrower ruling #4] — but that ruling doesn't tell us whether the once-per-turn limit resets when the ability is lost and regained.

What's missing: a rule (or ruling) on how per-turn activation restrictions are tracked — on the permanent that activated the ability, or on the specific ability/source — and whether losing and regaining the ability resets it. Without that, I won't guess. Nothing in the provided material distinguishes two-player from multiplayer play here either.

Side note that is grounded in the card text: only Sensei's Divining Top's {1} ability rearranges the top three cards; its {T} ability draws a card and puts Sensei's Divining Top itself on top of its owner's library, so use the {1} ability for both reorderings.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.401.6: If an effect causes a player to play with the top card of their library revealed, and that particular card stops being revealed for any length of time before being revealed again, it becomes a new object.
gold_text.602.5c: A player can’t begin to activate an ability that’s prohibited from being activated. If an object acquires an activated ability with a restriction on its use from another object, that restriction applies only to that ability as acquired from that object. It doesn’t apply to other, identically worded abilities.

answer_gold: Yes. Putrid Leech stopped being revealed for a time, so it is no longer the same object that it was before. Skill Borrower has a new ability that just has the same text as the ability that was activated earlier.

question: Noah controls a [Mons's Goblin Raiders] enchanted with a [Spider Umbra]. Alexandra casts [Yamabushi's Flame], targeting Mons's Goblin Raiders. What happens?
answer:
Direct answer (unchanged): Mons's Goblin Raiders survives; Spider Umbra is destroyed instead, and Mons's Goblin Raiders is not exiled.

On your challenge: you're right that none of the numbered Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given cover this interaction. The provided rules text is about choosing targets (115.1c, 115.1d, 115.5, 115.9, 115.9b, 115.10), triggered-ability wording and "looks back in time" triggers (603.1a, 603.10, 603.10a, 603.10d, 603.10e, 603.10f), attacking reselection (508.7c), gift (702.174m), and mentor (702.134c). None of those address replacement effects, destruction, lethal damage, or umbra armor, so I am not citing any of them — doing so would be a fake citation.

What does settle it is the authoritative card text and rulings I was given. Spider Umbra's printed umbra armor text reads: "If enchanted creature would be destroyed, instead remove all damage from it and destroy this Aura." Mons's Goblin Raiders is a 2/2 while enchanted (1/1 plus +1/+1). Yamabushi's Flame deals it 3 damage, which is lethal, and the game rules regarding lethal damage would destroy it — [Spider Umbra ruling #0] confirms that in the lethal-damage case it is those game rules, not the spell, that cause Spider Umbra to be destroyed instead. That replacement is mandatory [Spider Umbra ruling #6] and applies whatever the reason for destruction [Spider Umbra ruling #4]: all damage is removed from Mons's Goblin Raiders and Spider Umbra is destroyed instead.

Because the destruction is replaced, Mons's Goblin Raiders never dies, so Yamabushi's Flame's clause "If a creature dealt damage this way would die this turn, exile it instead" never applies. Mons's Goblin Raiders remains on the battlefield as a 1/1 with no damage marked, untapped and still in combat if it was in combat, since umbra armor is not regeneration [Spider Umbra ruling #3]. Spider Umbra goes to Noah's graveyard.

Caveat: for the rest of the turn Yamabushi's Flame's exile effect covers only the damage it dealt, and with Spider Umbra gone, later lethal damage from another source would kill Mons's Goblin Raiders normally. Nothing here depends on player count, so the result is identical in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.616.1g: If two or more replacement and/or prevention effects are attempting to modify the way an event affects an object or player, the affected object’s controller (or its owner if it has no controller) or the affected player chooses one to apply, following the steps listed below. If two or more players have to make these choices at the same time, choices are made in APNAP order (see rule 101.4). While following the steps in 616.1a–f, one replacement or prevention effect may apply to an event, and another may apply to an event contained within the first event. In this case, the second effect can’t be chosen until after the first effect has been chosen. A player is instructed to create a token that’s a copy of Voice of All, which has the ability “As this creature enters, choose a color.” Doubling Season has an ability that reads “If an effect would create one or more tokens under your control, it creates twice that many of those tokens instead.” Because entering the battlefield is an event contained within the event of creating a token, the effect of Doubling Season must be applied first, and then the effects of the two Voice of All tokens may be applied in either order.
gold_text.701.8a: Destroy To destroy a permanent, move it from the battlefield to its owner’s graveyard.
gold_text.702.89a: Umbra Armor Umbra armor is a static ability that appears on some Auras. “Umbra armor” means “If enchanted permanent would be destroyed, instead remove all damage marked on it and destroy this Aura.”

answer_gold:
Spider Umbra is destroyed and Mons's Goblin Raiders remains on the battlefield.

There are two replacement effects trying to apply to the same event. Umbra armor is attempting to replace the destruction of the creature, while Yamabushi's Flame's effect is attempting to replace where the creature moves to. The "move to the graveyard" event is a part of the "destroy" event, so the umbra armor replacement effect must apply first. Once that effect has been applied, the creature is no longer about to die, so there are no more effects to apply.

If the Mons's Goblin Raiders would die later in the turn, the Yamabushi's Flame's replacement effect will apply at that time and cause it to move to exile instead of the graveyard.

question: At the beginning of the game, Alex announced [Kaheera, the Orphanguard] as their companion. During the game, Alex cast [Carrion Grub] from their sideboard with [Wish]. Later, Alex restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. What happens?
answer:
Honest answer: the Comprehensive Rules text I was given does not cover this question. The numbered rules provided here are all about activating abilities (602.5, 602.5a–c, 117.1b, 801.6, 113.6j, 113.10a), Auras (303.4e), linked abilities (607.5), "look back in time" triggers (603.10d), costs in "if you do" clauses (118.12), opponents making choices (602.3), controlling another player (723.8), and "can't" beating "can" (101.2a). None of them address restarting a game, the pregame procedure, companions, or playing cards from outside the game, so I can't ground this answer in the provided rules text.

What the provided card rulings do say (offered as context, not as a CR citation): a game restarted by Karn Liberated immediately ends the old game and a new game begins with a normal pregame procedure, so a companion would be declared fresh, and only non-Aura permanent cards exiled with Karn Liberated's +4 or −3 stay in exile to be put onto the battlefield [Karn Liberated ruling #12] [Karn Liberated ruling #9] [Karn Liberated ruling #6] [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #3]. Also, once Carrion Grub was played from outside the game with Wish it behaves like any other card brought into the game [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #11] [Wish ruling #0], and players can't move cards between deck and sideboard before the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #5].

What is genuinely unsettled by everything I was given: which zone Carrion Grub occupies for the new game (back outside the game, or shuffled into Alex's new starting deck). That determines whether Alex's starting deck still meets Kaheera, the Orphanguard's companion requirement — Carrion Grub is an Insect, not a Cat, Elemental, Nightmare, Dinosaur, or Beast — and the requirement is checked only against the starting deck, not the sideboard [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #2]. I won't guess at that. Note also that with more than two players, a player who had already left before the restart isn't in the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #11].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.103.2b: Some games require additional steps that are taken after the starting player has been determined. Perform the actions listed in 103.2a–e in order, as applicable. If any players wish to reveal a card with a companion ability that they own from outside the game, they may do so. A player may reveal no more than one card this way, and they may do so only if their deck fulfills the condition of that card’s companion ability. The revealed card remains outside the game. (See rule 702.139, “Companion.”)
gold_text.726.2: There are three inherent triggered abilities associated with having the initiative. These triggered abilities have no source and are controlled by the player who had the initiative at the time the abilities triggered. This is an exception to rule 113.8. The full text of these abilities are “At the beginning of the upkeep of the player who has the initiative, that player ventures into Undercity,” “Whenever one or more creatures a player controls deal combat damage to the player who has the initiative, the controller of those creatures takes the initiative,” and “Whenever a player takes the initiative, that player ventures into Undercity.” See rule 701.49, “Venture into the Dungeon.”

answer_gold: Carrion Grub will be shuffled into Alex's library along with the rest of the cards in the game. Because Carrion Grub violates Kaheera, the Orphanguard's companion restriction, Alex can't announce it as their companion for the restarted game.
